posts.name: Eric Adams
posts.text:
There is a reason New York City has not experienced the kind of violent riots we have witnessed in Paris and other major cities around the world.

We had the NYPD’s Strategic Response Group (SRG), a specialized unit of highly trained officers prepared to confront violence before it spiraled out of control.

Let me make something absolutely clear.

Peaceful protest is a constitutional right. Violent rioting is a crime. And confusing the two is a dangerous failure of leadership.

The SRG was not created to silence peaceful protesters. It was created to protect New Yorkers when demonstrations crossed the line into violence, to protect businesses from destruction, peaceful demonstrators from violent agitators, and police officers from being assaulted.

Now City Hall is dismantling that specialized unit, introducing unarmed civilian de-escalation teams, and restricting the tools available to police.

I support de-escalation. Every responsible police officer does. But de-escalation is a strategy, not a substitute for the ability to confront violence.

You cannot reason with a brick flying through a storefront. You cannot negotiate with a Molotov cocktail. And you cannot send a social worker to do the job of a specially trained police officer confronting a violent mob.

The NYPD will still have officers responding to protests. But the question City Hall  has failed to answer is why New Yorkers will be safer without a dedicated unit specifically trained for these dangerous situations.

What happens when peaceful protesters are attacked? When businesses are being destroyed? When police officers are surrounded and assaulted?

Who responds? How quickly? With what training? And with what tools?

These are not hypothetical questions. These are the decisions that determine whether a dangerous situation is contained or an entire neighborhood descends into chaos.

I spent four years as mayor and 22 years as an NYPD officer. I know the difference between protecting someone’s right to protest and allowing someone to use that protest as cover for violence.

The right to protest does not include the right to terrorize. And protecting civil liberties should never require surrendering public safety.

City Hall may believe dismantling the SRG is a political victory.

But if violence erupts, the people paying the price won’t be the activists applauding this announcement or the politicians celebrating it at City Hall.

It will be the police officer who gets assaulted. The small-business owner whose livelihood is destroyed. The peaceful protester who gets caught in the violence. The innocent New Yorker who simply wants to get home safely.

New York City’s Public Safety is not a laboratory for ideological experiments. Our police officers are not expendable. And public safety is not something you gamble with to score political points.

City Hall should reverse this decision before New Yorkers discover the consequences the hard way.

I love this story about what George Clooney learned from moving to Italy:

In the early-2000s he was a motorcycle trip to the Italian Alps and stopped by a small town on Lake Como to visit some friends. After he left his bike broke down so Clooney knocked on the door of the nearest house (which happened to be a beautiful estate on the water).

A member of the Heinz ketchup dynasty owned it. By the end of the day, Heinz asked the actor if he would like to buy the lakeside estate. Clooney balked which caused Heinz to lower the price.

Clooney said yes on a whim assuming he would sell the home within a year to turn a quick profit.

After moving in Clooney was sitting alone by the pool. In an interview with Esquire he described what happened next:

He looked out the window that first evening and saw a few construction workers walking home after work, orange vests, bellies sticking out, hard hats cocked on their heads. They pulled hunks off a loaf of bread and passed a bottle of wine as they walked, and they were singing.

Singing!

Clooney, who was making the leap from being pretty famous to being an international A-list actor–The Perfect Storm had been a hit, and Ocean’s Eleven was an even bigger one–thought to himself, Those guys are living their lives better than I am. Way better than I am.

He was always in such a hurry to be a success that he’d been eating dinner standing up for as long as he could remember. And then these guys–not much money, doing hard labor all day, and they’re celebrating another night walking home.

He thought, I’m never going to leave this house.

Clooney still has the house all these years later.

Some more thoughts about living a better life now:

posts.text:
NVDA reports tomorrow after the close.

The first print without Jensen Huang. The stock is down 28% in four weeks and sits 36% below its high. The quarter itself closed on October 25, two weeks before any of this started.

Street EPS: $2.47 
Street Revenue: $109.0B

Alphatica Estimates:
EPS: $2.56
Revenue: $112.5B

OUR CALL: BEAT ✅

THE LEADERSHIP CHANGE:

On November 12 the board announced that Huang resigned as President, CEO and director, effective immediately. That came four days after the board opened an independent investigation into his conduct.

CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO and remains CFO. Harvey Jones becomes the first Chair of the Board in the company's history. The board will consider internal and external candidates.

The board's only operating statement: it expects "operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption." The report and the call stay on schedule.

WHY THE BEAT:

The results are already locked. The quarter ended before the leadership news.

NVIDIA guided $108B, plus or minus 2%, with gross margin of 74%. That guide assumed no China data center compute. The street sits at $109.0B, just above the midpoint.

NVIDIA has beaten EPS 12 of the last 12 quarters by an average of 7.6%. It has beaten revenue 12 of 12, by 3.5% on average over the last four.

We are at $112.5B, 2% above the top of the guide and up 97% from a year ago. That gives us $2.56, a 3.6% beat and below NVIDIA's recent average.

One caution on the street number: The leadership change is not in it.

THE GUIDANCE QUESTION:

This is the number that matters tomorrow.

Kress has delivered NVIDIA's outlook on every call for years. Now she delivers it as CEO. The street wants $124.5B next quarter, up 14%. In August NVIDIA gave a preliminary outlook of about 70% revenue growth for next fiscal year, and the street's estimates lean on it.

There are three paths. Reaffirm both. Guide next quarter and pull or widen the longer-range view. Or widen everything. Companies in a leadership transition have reasons to commit to less. We are not calling which path. A pulled long-range outlook would be a disclosure decision, not a demand signal, and the call is where that difference gets explained.

THE NVIDIA CAPITAL NETWORK:

Our August report mapped 209 NVIDIA transactions across 290 counterparties, tied to $314.9B of aggregate round value. 95% of that sits on the demand side: the AI labs and cloud builders that buy NVIDIA's chips. Huang built it.

What the filings already show: the selling started before he left. Between June 30 and September 30, NVIDIA cut its Intel stake 25% and its Nokia stake 56%, and trimmed Synopsys. Its SpaceX position grew after the xAI stake converted. The 13F portfolio fell from $63.4B to $48.3B.

The demand side is mostly private and illiquid. It cannot be sold quickly even if someone wanted to. Q2 showed $25B of outstanding investment commitments.

WHAT THE PORTFOLIO DOES TO EPS:

Same work we ran on GOOGL. We marked NVIDIA's public holdings across the fiscal quarter.

July 24 to October 23: SpaceX up 28%, the biggest driver. CoreWeave down 25%, Coherent down 26%, Intel down 6%. Net, our estimate is a $1.8B to $3.7B gain on the public book.

Two points. First, these marks hit GAAP only. NVIDIA's adjusted EPS, the number the street measures, excludes them. In Q2 it excluded $7.8B of equity gains. Expect GAAP to run above adjusted again. Second, the $47.9B private book is marked on its own schedule and we cannot see it.

Since the quarter closed it has turned. Intel is down 36% and SpaceX is off its October level. At today's prices the public book is down about $6.7B, roughly 22 cents of GAAP EPS. That lands in the February report, not tomorrow's.

OUR FOUR SIGNALS:

Earnings Quality: 5/6 BULLISH, unchanged. Scored on the FY2026 10-K. Revenue $215.9B, net income $120.1B. Stock compensation fell to 3.0% of revenue from 10.0% three years ago. Management's internal accounting signals improved sha

Under the new rule, chip designers in China and other restricted regions can no longer qualify for an exemption through the existing transistor-count verification process unless they have BIS status as an “approved” or “authorized” IC designer. Under the previous rule, a foundry or an outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) provider could verify the transistor count to establish eligibility for an exemption. Now, BIS itself has to decide whether to grant one.

As a result, foundries such as TSMC and Samsung Electronics, as well as OSAT providers such as ASE and Amkor, will need to conduct more thorough background checks on their customers.

Don’t Hike Into a Mirage: Wall Street’s March Rate Rise Would Land on a Energy Glut

Wall Street wants the Fed to hike into March. The energy glut and the base effects say that would be a mistake.

The glut is already showing up at the pump. Wholesale gasoline futures for December delivery closed at $2.53 a gallon today, down 18.4% in four weeks and 20% from the late-October high of $3.18. Today alone they fell 3.4%, to a fresh one-month low. 

This is the physical market confirming what the IEA already reported: supply above demand for the first time since the Iran war began, inventories up 52m barrels in October, and Brent 30% off its peak. Retail prices follow wholesale with a lag of a few weeks.

Headline CPI is about to look hot for the wrong reason. Even with pump prices flat, inflation climbs from 3.7% to about 4.1% by January, only because it’s measured against last winter’s cheap gasoline. That’s arithmetic, not new inflation. Excluding gasoline, inflation is already running at 2.8%.

Then the math flips. In March, the spring 2026 war spike drops out of the comparison, and headline falls by about three-quarters of a point in a single month. 

With wholesale already down 20%, our steepest scenario is now the one playing out, and it takes headline inflation to about 1.7% by May, below the Fed’s target.

So the Street is asking the Fed to tighten at the peak of a statistical illusion, into a gasoline market already in free fall. Hiking into March means tightening into the steepest drop in headline inflation of the cycle. That isn’t prudence. It’s driving by the rear-view mirror.

The Fed shouldn’t take its cue from Wall Street’s fear of a January print. It should look through it.

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
I like Lyn's work but it's wrong to say bank deposit creation is "IOU" creation and not money creation. That treats state money as the only real money. It's an excessively government-centric view of how money gets created, a mistake MMT ironically makes too. Reserves sit above deposits in the settlement hierarchy, but that doesn't make deposits any less money.

It's fine to say deposits are an IOU, but deposits are absolutely money. They're the money households and businesses actually hold and spend, and they're accepted virtually everywhere. Banks make loans, which create deposits, and find the reserves after the fact. Reserve balances don't constrain lending for well-capitalized banks.

And it's not the bank's IOUs that "fail at scale." A loan creates two IOUs: the borrower's loan, which is the bank's asset, and the deposit, which is the bank's liability. It's the assets that fail, not the deposits. Asset losses are a capital problem and the Fed can't print capital. Deposit runs are a liquidity problem, and the Fed lends reserves against collateral. SVB had discount window access and still failed because unrealized securities losses had already wiped out most of its capital on a market value basis. Capital, not reserves, is the constraint for banks. Banks don't lever reserves. They lever their capital.

This matters for understanding the plumbing of the money system because deposits get created two main ways: when banks lend or buy securities, and when the Fed buys assets from nonbanks. Both are money creation, with different economic impacts. Treating bank lending as IOU stacking on top of state money diminishes how banks are major money creators in their own right and why the Fed interacts with them the way it does.

quoted.text:
Banks don't lend reserves. They lever reserves and make IOUs on top of them, rather than "creating money."

But then whenever those IOUs start to fail at scale, the central bank creates more reserves for them.

Over the past 50 years, if the US central bank held reserves flat and banks kept making money, there'd be a 160-to-1 ratio between deposits and reserves, which would be untenable. However, whenever it comes even slightly untenable, the central bank creates more reserves and swaps them for assets from banks, boosting the ratio and giving banks more lending/leveraging ability to keep it growing.

The US bank deposit-to-reserve ratio is under 4-to-1 because the central bank accommodates bank lending by creating new reserves.

The employment index improved primarily because fewer firms were cutting workers, not because hiring suddenly accelerated. Only 21.5% reported adding employees, while 75.1% reported no change. Meanwhile, new orders collapsed from 23.2 to just 3.0, with firms reporting rising orders plunging from 42.9% to 28.3%. 

Now examine the historical chart. Notice how previous peaks in manufacturing employment and hours were followed by sharp reversals, particularly around economic downturns. That happens because employment typically lags demand. Manufacturers maintain staffing to fulfill existing orders until weakening demand forces them to reduce hours and eventually headcount. 

Not every peak signals a recession, but celebrating employment strength while ignoring collapsing orders completely misses the possibility that today’s strongest labor readings are tomorrow’s lagging indicators of economic deterioration.

posts.text:
Empire State Manufacturing Survey Exposes A Troubling Disconnect Between Optimism And Reality

The New York Fed’s November survey reveals deteriorating demand beneath a positive headline. Business conditions plunged from 25.5 to 7.8, missing expectations of 18.0. Only 31% reported improvement, 23.2% deterioration and 45.8% no change.

Demand Is Losing Momentum

New orders collapsed from 23.2 to 3.0. Firms reporting rising orders fell from 42.9% to 28.3%, while those reporting declines rose from 19.7% to 25.2%. Another 46.5% saw no change. Declining orders nearly matched rising orders.

Shipments slowed from 13.1 to 8.8, unfilled orders from 14.0 to 10.3 and inventories from 11.6 to 9.2. All remain positive, but incoming demand is weakening faster than ongoing activity. Earlier orders may be sustaining current activity.

Employment Strength Has A Catch

Employment reached 18.1, its highest since June 2022, and the workweek index rose to 13.5. Yet firms adding workers barely increased from 20% to 21.5%. Most improvement came from firms cutting employment falling from 9.8% to 3.4%. Another 75.1% reported unchanged staffing.

That is stronger retention, not a hiring boom. If orders stay weak, hiring freezes and reduced hours may precede layoffs.

Inflation Is Slowing, Not Disappearing

Prices paid fell from 59.5 to 45.9 and prices received from 30.6 to 27.2. The share reporting price declines rounded to zero. Cost inflation moderated, not reversed.

Supply availability remained negative at minus 9.2 and deliveries continued lengthening. During the survey window WTI fell around 9.7% while natural gas rose about 13.8%. Future input price expectations remained at 66.7 versus 41.2 for selling prices, raising pricing power concerns.

The Contradiction Few Are Examining

Future business expectations rose from 21.0 to 28.9 and capital spending intentions to 23.0, their highest since December 2022.

Yet firms expecting higher future shipments fell from 50.4% to 41.4%, those anticipating more hiring declined from 34.5% to 27.4%, and expected unfilled orders dropped from 14.0 to 2.3. Even the share expecting higher new orders declined from 46.6% to 45.2%.

The optimism reflects fewer pessimists more than stronger demand.

Businesses invest not only to expand production but also to survive deteriorating conditions. Automation, energy efficient machinery and equipment that reduces labor costs can raise capital spending even as future hiring and demand weaken.

My strongest suspicion is that some investment plans are defensive, not expansionary. The survey does not identify their purpose, but portraying higher capex intentions as proof of stronger demand while fewer firms anticipate more shipments and hiring is misleading.

The Broader Reality

October ISM manufacturing remained expansionary at 55.5 and manufacturing payrolls added 19,000 jobs, although hours were flat. Philadelphia and Dallas also reported sharp order slowdowns, while tighter small business credit threatens investment.

The Bottom Line

Businesses may be investing to protect profitability and reduce future labor needs while incoming orders weaken. Such investment can support GDP without generating a durable expansion in employment or output.

This is not proof of a manufacturing recession. It is a fragile expansion whose current employment and shipments could become lagging indicators if orders fail to recover. Greater optimism should not be confused with greater economic strength.

FORMER ROBINHOOD ENGINEER PLEADS GUILTY TO FRAUD OVER HYPERLIQUID TRADES

Huaisong Xiang, a former Robinhood software engineer, pleaded guilty to wire fraud and agreed to forfeit $125,523 in illicit trading profits.

Between 2025 and 2026, he used confidential information about upcoming Robinhood Crypto listings to repeatedly buy perpetual futures on Hyperliquid before the public announcements.

Xiang traded contracts tied to cryptocurrencies he knew Robinhood was planning to list, profiting from information that was not yet available to the public.

He faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison, with sentencing scheduled for February 25, 2027.
